items.prompt: Which command prints the full path of the directory you are currently in?
rubric: `pwd` stands for print working directory.
`ls` lists contents and `whoami` shows the username, so learners who mix up 'where' and 'what' pick them.

items.prompt: Which command creates a new, empty directory?
rubric: `mkdir` makes directories.
`touch` creates files, and `rmdir` removes directories, which confuses learners who half-remember the names.

items.prompt: What does the command `cp a.txt b.txt` do?

options.label: Compares a.txt with b.txt line by line
Renames a.txt to b.txt, removing the old name

rubric: `cp` copies a file.
Renaming is `mv`, and comparing is `diff`.

items.prompt: Which symbol sends the output of one command into the input of another?
rubric: The pipe `|` connects stdout of one command to stdin of the next.
`>` redirects to a file instead, and `;` just runs commands in sequence.

items.prompt: Which command opens the manual page (man page) for a command such as `ls`?
rubric: `man` shows manual pages.
`doc` is not a standard command, and `help` is for shell builtins only.

items.prompt: Which commands can display the contents of a text file? Select all that apply.
rubric: `cat`, `less` and `head` all show file contents, fully or in part.
`cd` changes directory and `mkdir` makes one; neither reads files.

items.prompt: Ana is deep inside /var/log/apache2 on a Linux server. She wants to jump straight back to her own home directory with a single short command. Which command should she type?
rubric: `~` is shorthand for the current user's home directory.
`cd ..` only goes up one level, `cd /` goes to root, and `cd .` stays put.

items.prompt: You run `echo hi > f.txt` twice in a row. What does f.txt contain afterwards?

options.label: The word hi on two lines
An error, since the file already exists

rubric: `>` overwrites the file each time, so only one `hi` remains.
Two lines would come from `>>`, which appends.

items.prompt: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-xr--` for a file. What can users who are neither the owner nor in the group do?

options.label: Execute it but not read it

rubric: The last three characters `r--` are the permissions for others: read only.
Learners who read the wrong triplet choose the group's `r-x` or the owner's `rwx`.

items.prompt: What does `grep error log.txt | wc -l` output?

options.label: The total number of lines in log.txt
The size of log.txt in bytes
The number of words in log.txt
The number of lines containing error

rubric: `grep` keeps only matching lines, and `wc -l` counts those lines.
Counting all lines ignores the filter that the pipe applies.

items.prompt: Which of these is an absolute path?
rubric: An absolute path starts at the root with `/`.
The others depend on the current directory, so they are relative paths.

items.prompt: Why is it risky to run `rm notes.txt` on a file you may still need?

options.label: It only hides the file until the next reboot, then deletes it
It asks the file's owner to confirm before it deletes anything
It moves the file into a hidden trash folder that empties daily
It deletes the file at once, with no trash to restore it from

rubric: `rm` unlinks the file immediately and the shell has no recycle bin.
Learners used to desktop trash assume deletion is reversible.

items.prompt: After running `chmod 644 report.txt`, which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: The owner can read the file
Other users can write to the file
The owner can write to the file

rubric: Mode 6 gives the owner read and write; 4 gives group and others read only.
No one gets execute or other-user write, so those options are wrong.

items.prompt: Lee has a file backup.sh in the current directory. Running `./backup.sh` prints 'Permission denied', although `cat backup.sh` works fine. What is the most likely explanation?

options.label: The shell cannot run files ending in .sh
The file lacks the execute permission bit
Scripts can only be run by the root user
The file is stored in the wrong directory

rubric: Reading works but running fails, which points to a missing `x` bit; `chmod +x` fixes it.
If the file were in the wrong directory the error would be 'No such file'.

items.prompt: A file `log.txt` already has content. How does `echo hi >> log.txt` differ from `echo hi > log.txt`?

options.label: `>>` replaces the file's content; `>` adds the text at the end
`>>` shows the text on screen and saves it; `>` only saves it
`>>` fails if the file exists; `>` creates a new file only
`>>` adds the text at the end; `>` replaces the file's content

rubric: `>>` appends while `>` truncates and overwrites.
Swapping them is the most common mix-up.

items.prompt: In the command `ls | wc -l`, what does the pipe symbol do?

options.label: Saves the output of `ls` into a file called `wc`
Runs `wc -l` first and then passes its result to `ls`
Feeds the output of `ls` into `wc -l` as its input
Runs `wc -l` only if `ls` finishes without any errors

rubric: A pipe connects stdout of the left command to stdin of the right one.
Distractors confuse pipes with file redirection or with `&&`.

items.prompt: `ls -l` shows `-rwxr-x---` for a file. What does this permission string mean?

options.label: Owner can read and write only; group can execute; others have full access
Everyone can read and execute; only the owner can write to the file
Owner has full access; group can read and write; others can read
Owner has full access; group can read and execute; others have none

rubric: The three triplets are owner, group, others: rwx, r-x, ---.
Distractors misread the order or the dashes.

items.prompt: Which of these is an absolute path?
rubric: An absolute path starts at the root `/`.
Others depend on the current directory.

items.prompt: After running a command in bash, `echo $?` prints `0`. What does that tell you?

options.label: The last command printed no output at all
The last command was run as process number 0
The last command ran with zero arguments

rubric: `$?` holds the exit status of the previous command; 0 means success.
Distractors mistake it for output, argument count or process ID.

items.prompt: Which commands only display information and do not change or delete any file? Select all that apply.
rubric: `cat`, `ls -l` and `head` only read and show data.
`rm` deletes and `mv` renames or moves files.

items.prompt: Ana is in `/home/ana`. `ls` shows a directory named `Projects`. She types `cd projects` and gets: `No such file or directory`. What best explains the error?

options.label: Directories inside her home folder need `sudo` before `cd` can enter them
Linux file names are case-sensitive, so `projects` is not `Projects`
The directory name must end with a trailing slash for `cd` to find it
A relative name fails in `cd`, so she must type `/home/ana/projects`

rubric: Linux treats `Projects` and `projects` as different names.
Other options invent rules about absolute paths, sudo or slashes.

items.prompt: What are the permissions of a file after `chmod 640 report.txt`?
rubric: 6 = rw-, 4 = r--, 0 = ---, for owner, group, others.
Distractors misconvert the octal digits.

items.prompt: Which command counts how many lines of `log.txt` contain the word `error`?
rubric: grep filters matching lines, and wc -l counts them.
Others swap grep's arguments or misuse wc and redirection.

items.prompt: You want both normal output and error messages of `./job` saved to `out.txt`. Which command does that?
rubric: `> out.txt 2>&1` sends stdout to the file and stderr to the same place.
The first two capture only one stream; piping to a file is invalid.

items.prompt: `./backup.sh` gives `Permission denied`, and `ls -l` shows `-rw-r--r--` for it. Which command fixes this?
rubric: The script lacks the execute bit, which `chmod +x` adds.
Others remove permission, move or delete the file.

items.prompt: What does `for f in a b c; do echo "$f.txt"; done` print?
rubric: The loop sets f to each word in turn, and `$f` expands to it.
Distractors ignore expansion or the loop.

items.prompt: `notes.txt` does not exist in the current directory. Which commands create it as an empty or text file? Select all that apply.
rubric: `touch` and redirection with `>` create a regular file.
`cat` and `ls` only error; `mkdir` makes a directory.

items.prompt: Lee's current directory is `/home/lee/docs`, which contains `report.txt`. A sibling directory `/home/lee/archive` exists. Lee wants a copy of the report in the archive without changing directory.
rubric: `..` moves up to `/home/lee`, so `../archive/` is the sibling directory.
`archive/` would look inside docs; the others use wrong source paths.

items.prompt: Several `.log` files sit in the current directory. Which command prints the total number of lines containing `ERROR` across all of them as a single number?
rubric: `grep -h` prints only the matching lines, with no filename prefix, and `wc -l` counts them in total.
`grep -c` gives one count per file, and `grep -l` makes `wc` count matching files rather than lines.

items.prompt: A file `report.txt` has mode `640`, owner `alice` and group `dev`. User `bob` is a member of `dev` but is not alice. What can bob do with the file?

options.label: Nothing, because he is not the owner

rubric: Mode 640 gives the group read (4) only, and bob matches the group class.
Distractors confuse the group digit with the owner digit or assume non-owners get nothing.

items.prompt: `data.txt` contains these lines, one per line: a, b, a, c, b, a. What does `sort data.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -1` print (ignoring leading spaces)?
rubric: Sorting groups identical lines, `uniq -c` counts them, and the numeric reverse sort puts the most frequent first: 3 a.
`6 a` confuses the total line count with a's count, and the others are lower-frequency entries.

items.prompt: You run `ls /nonexistent /tmp > out.txt 2> err.txt`. Where does the output end up?

options.label: Both go to the screen, because `ls` writes directly to the terminal
The `/tmp` listing goes to `out.txt`; the error goes to `err.txt`
Both the listing and the error go to `err.txt`, as the last redirection wins
The `/tmp` listing goes to `err.txt`; the error goes to `out.txt`

rubric: `>` redirects stdout (file descriptor 1) and `2>` redirects stderr, so the listing and the error are separated.
Distractors swap the streams or assume stderr is merged into stdout.

items.prompt: What does this do to a file named `notes.txt`? `for f in *.txt; do mv "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"; done`

options.label: Fails because `mv` cannot rename inside a loop

rubric: `${f%.txt}` strips the shortest matching suffix `.txt`, and `.md` is then appended.
Distractors misread the `%` suffix removal as an append or reorder.

items.prompt: The directory `a` does not exist yet. Which commands create `a/b/c` in a single command, including the missing parents? Select all that apply.
rubric: `mkdir -p`, its long form `--parents`, and `install -d` all create missing parent directories.
Plain `mkdir` fails when the parent is missing, and `-r` is not a valid `mkdir` option.

items.prompt: You are writing `backup.sh`, which is run as `./backup.sh /data`. The script must print a usage message to stderr and stop with a non-zero status when no argument is given. Which snippet at the top of the script does this?
rubric: `$1` is the first argument; `-z` tests for empty, and `>&2` with `exit 1` reports the error properly.
Distractors test the wrong variable (`$0` is the script name), invert the test, or exit with status 0.

items.prompt: In a directory containing `a.log` and `b.log`, `find . -name *.log` fails with an error about the expression. What is the cause?

options.label: GNU `find` requires the starting path to come after the `-name` test, not before it
`find` cannot match a file extension with `-name` unless the `-regex` option is also given
The shell expands unquoted `*.log` to `a.log b.log` before `find` runs
`find` requires `-type f` whenever `-name` is used to match files by a pattern

rubric: The shell expands the unquoted glob first, so `find` receives extra arguments; quoting `'*.log'` lets `find` do the matching.
Distractors invent syntax requirements that `find` does not have.

items.prompt: `sudo echo "x" >> /etc/myapp.conf` fails with "Permission denied", although sudo itself succeeded. Why?

options.label: `echo` is a shell builtin, so sudo cannot run it and the write falls back to your user
`>>` appends are blocked on files in `/etc` unless the file was created by root
Your unprivileged shell opens the redirect target before sudo runs `echo`
`sudo` drops root privileges once the command starts writing to standard output

rubric: Redirections are performed by the invoking shell, so the file is opened without root rights; `echo x | sudo tee -a` avoids this.
Distractors blame the builtin, the operator, or invented sudo behaviour.

items.prompt: A cleanup script contains `cd /srv/app/tmp; rm -rf *`. One night it deleted files in the user's home directory, where the cron job started. What is the root cause?

options.label: The `;` runs `rm` even when `cd` fails, so `*` expanded in the original directory
`rm -rf` resolves `*` against the script's own directory rather than the shell's, so it hit home
Cron jobs run with root privileges, so `rm` could reach the home directory despite the `cd`
`*` also matches directories outside the current one when `-r` is set, so `rm` followed it up

rubric: With `;` the second command runs regardless of the first; `cd ... && rm` or `set -e` prevents it.
Distractors misattribute the failure to `rm`, cron privileges, or glob scope.

items.prompt: This script prints an empty line instead of the line count: `cat list.txt | while read l; do count=$((count+1)); done; echo $count`. What explains it?

options.label: The pipe runs the loop in a subshell, so `count` is lost afterwards
`read` consumes all of the piped input at once, so the loop body never runs
`echo` runs in parallel with the loop and prints before the loop has finished
`$((count+1))` fails on an unset variable, so `count` is never assigned

rubric: Each pipeline stage runs in a subshell in bash, so variable changes in the loop don't reach the parent; use `done < list.txt`.
Unset variables are treated as 0 in arithmetic, and `echo` runs after the pipeline finishes.

items.prompt: `ls -l run.sh` shows `-rwxr-xr-x`, yet `./run.sh` reports "bad interpreter: No such file or directory" for a shebang that is visibly `#!/bin/bash`. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: `/bin/bash` is a symlink to another binary, and the kernel does not follow links in shebang paths
The file has Windows CRLF line endings, so the interpreter name ends in a carriage return
The file is on a filesystem mounted noexec, so the kernel cannot load the interpreter named in the shebang
The shebang line is not the first line because of a hidden blank line, so the kernel ignores it

rubric: A trailing `\r` makes the kernel look for `/bin/bash\r`, which doesn't exist; convert with `dos2unix` or `sed`.
Permissions would give a different error, and shebangs can point to symlinks.

items.prompt: A script has `if [ $name = "bob" ]; then ...` and fails with "unary operator expected" when `name` is empty. Which changes fix the failure? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add `set -e` at the top of the script

rubric: An unquoted empty variable vanishes, leaving `[ = bob ]`; quoting or using `[[ ]]` avoids word splitting.
Removing the spaces breaks the test, and `set -e` only changes error exit behaviour.

items.prompt: You run `grep ERROR app.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn` to find the most common error. Every line shows a count of 1, though the same message clearly repeats hundreds of times. Each log line starts with a timestamp, like `2024-05-01 10:02:11 ERROR disk full`. What is the cause?

options.label: `uniq -c` only counts lines that contain digits, so ERROR lines stay at 1
`sort` runs before `uniq` and collapses duplicate lines, so counts reset
`grep` prints each distinct matching message once and ignores repeats
Timestamps make every line unique, so `uniq` finds no identical lines

rubric: `uniq` compares whole lines, so differing timestamps prevent grouping; strip them first, for example with `cut -d' ' -f3-`.
Distractors misdescribe `uniq`, `sort` and `grep` behaviour.

items.prompt: A script runs `make 2>&1 > build.log`. Error messages still appear on the terminal and are missing from build.log. Why?

options.label: Redirections are processed left to right, so stderr was pointed at the terminal's stdout before stdout went to the file
make opens /dev/tty directly for its error output, and shell redirection can only capture streams that go through file descriptors 1 and 2
The `2>&1` form only works when stdout is a pipe, so with a file target stderr is silently left on the terminal
Redirections are processed right to left, so stdout was sent to the file first and stderr was then duplicated onto the old terminal stdout

rubric: The shell applies redirections in order, so `2>&1` copies the terminal destination of stdout before it is changed.
Distractors assume right-to-left processing or a pipe-only restriction.

items.prompt: A directory has `my notes.txt` and `todo.txt`. The loop `for f in *.txt; do wc -l $f; done` prints `wc: my: No such file or directory`. What is the cause?

options.label: The for loop splits its list on newlines only, which drops the text after the first space in each name
wc cannot read files whose names contain spaces unless they are first passed through `ls`
The unquoted `$f` is word-split after expansion, so wc receives `my` and `notes.txt` as two arguments
The glob splits filenames at spaces, so the loop variable receives `my` and `notes.txt` as separate values

rubric: Globbing keeps each name intact; the split happens when the unquoted variable is expanded.
Distractors blame the glob or the loop rather than the missing quotes.

items.prompt: As a normal user with working sudo rights, you run `sudo echo 'x' >> /etc/app.conf` and get Permission denied. Why?

options.label: The shell opens /etc/app.conf for appending as your user before sudo starts echo, so the open fails
sudo resets the working directory, so the path /etc/app.conf resolves to a different place
The `>>` operator needs the group membership of root, which sudo does not pass to child processes
echo is a shell builtin, so sudo cannot elevate it and silently ignores the command

rubric: Redirection is set up by the invoking shell, not by the command run under sudo.
Distractors invent builtin, group or path explanations.

items.prompt: A script runs `grep ERROR /var/log/missing.log | sort > errors.txt; echo $?` and prints 0 even though grep failed because the file does not exist. What explains this?

options.label: Without `pipefail`, the pipeline's status is that of its last command, sort, which succeeded
`$?` is only updated by commands that print to the terminal, so it keeps its earlier value of 0
grep returns 0 whenever it writes its error message to stderr instead of stdout, even on failure
The redirection `> errors.txt` resets `$?` to 0 once the output file has been created successfully

rubric: The default pipeline status is the last command's status, hiding the failure of grep.
Distractors misattribute the 0 to grep, the redirect or how `$?` is updated.

items.prompt: A script runs `count=0; cat data.txt | while read -r line; do count=$((count+1)); done; echo $count` and prints 0 for a 50-line file. What is the cause?

options.label: `read -r` consumes the whole file in a single call, so the loop body never executes even once
`$((count+1))` is evaluated once at parse time, so count is never updated on later loop iterations
The loop runs in a subshell, so the increments change a copy of the variable that is discarded
`cat` keeps the file open and holds its lock, so the while loop sees end-of-file immediately

rubric: The loop runs in a subshell, so its changes to `count` never reach the parent shell.
Distractors suggest the loop never runs or arithmetic is fixed at parse time.

items.prompt: A directory `d` has mode `r--` (no execute) for the user running the commands, and contains `a.txt`, which that user may read. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: `ls -l d` reports errors when reading the entries' details
A new file can be created in `d` as long as the user owns the directory
`cd d` succeeds because read permission is enough to enter a directory
`ls d` can list the names of the entries in `d`

rubric: Read lets you list names; execute (search) is needed to reach entries, stat them or cd into the directory.
Distractors treat read as enough to enter, or ownership as overriding the missing write bit.

items.prompt: A backup script calls `mytool`, which is installed in `/home/ana/bin` and found through a PATH line in `~/.bashrc`. Run from Ana's terminal it works. Run from her crontab it fails with `mytool: command not found`, although the file has the executable bit set. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: cron starts jobs with a minimal environment that does not read `~/.bashrc`, so PATH lacks `/home/ana/bin`
cron jobs have no controlling terminal, and commands installed in home directories can only be located with a tty
cron clears the executable bit of scripts it launches, so each command must be re-chmodded first
cron runs jobs as root, and root has no access to `/home/ana/bin`

rubric: Cron's environment is minimal and non-interactive, so PATH set in `~/.bashrc` is absent.
Distractors blame user identity, tty needs or permission bits.

items.prompt: Criteria: delete `*.tmp` regular files older than 7 days under `/data`; names may contain spaces or newlines; no risk of hitting argument-list limits; fewest moving parts. Which command is best?
rubric: `find -delete` handles any filename and spawns no argument lists or pipes.
Distractors rely on word splitting of find output, which breaks on spaces or newlines.

items.prompt: Criteria: a deployment script must stop at the first failing command, treat unset variables as errors, and fail when any stage of a pipeline fails. Which header meets all three?
rubric: `-e` stops on failure, `-u` flags unset variables, and `pipefail` exposes failures inside pipelines.
Each distractor omits one of the three requirements.

items.prompt: A 400 GB access log has about 600 million distinct client IPs; the host has 4 GB of RAM. Criteria: list the 10 most frequent IPs and finish without running out of memory. Which approach is best?

options.label: `for ip in $(cut -d' ' -f1 log | sort -u); do grep -c "$ip" log; done`
`awk '{c[$1]++} END{for(i in c) print c[i], i}' log | sort -rn | head -10`

rubric: `sort` spills to temporary files, so it works within limited RAM, unlike an in-memory awk array of 600 million keys.
Distractors hold all keys in memory, rescan the log per IP, or do not give counts per IP.

items.prompt: A cleanup script runs `rm -rf "$BUILD_DIR"/*`. If `BUILD_DIR` is unset it expands to `/*`. Criteria: abort before deleting anything when it is unset or empty, and keep it to one line. Which change is best?
rubric: `${VAR:?}` aborts with an error when the variable is unset or empty, before rm runs.
Distractors still expand to `/*`, or delete in the current directory when cd fails.

items.prompt: Criteria: members of group `devs` can read and write in `/srv/proj`; other users have no access; files created inside automatically belong to group `devs`. Which pair of commands meets all three?
rubric: Mode 2770 gives the group full access, excludes others, and setgid makes new files inherit the group.
Distractors lack setgid, let others read, or open the directory to everyone.

items.prompt: A script processes uploaded files whose names may contain spaces, newlines or a leading dash. Which practices are justified? Select all that apply.

options.label: Put `--` before filename arguments so names starting with `-` are not read as options
Run each name through `eval` so the shell re-parses special characters and handles them correctly
Quote every expansion, as in `"$f"`, so names are not split or globbed
Build the list with `for f in $(ls)` because `ls` escapes unusual characters in each name
Pass names from `find` to `xargs` with `-print0` and `-0`, so any name can be passed safely

rubric: Quoting, `--` and NUL-delimited lists each address a distinct failure mode with odd filenames.
`ls` output is still word-split, and `eval` adds injection risk.

items.prompt: A backup runs hourly from cron but sometimes takes 90 minutes, so runs overlap and corrupt the archive. Criteria: never run two at once, release the lock automatically if the job crashes or the host reboots, and add no extra daemon. Which fix fits best?

options.label: Have the script `touch /tmp/backup.lock` at the start and `rm` it at the end, skipping the run if the file already exists
Wrap the cron command as `flock -n /var/lock/backup.lock backup.sh`, since the kernel drops the lock when the process dies
Change the schedule to every two hours and add `sleep 600`, so overlap is unlikely under normal load
Have the script check `pgrep -f backup.sh` at the start and exit if any match is found, leaving no lock file behind

rubric: `flock` ties the lock to the process, so it is atomic and released on a crash or reboot.
A touch-file goes stale after a crash and is racy; pgrep can match itself; a longer schedule only makes overlap less likely.

items.prompt: A cleanup script must recursively delete every `*.tmp` file under the current directory. File names may contain spaces and even newlines. Judged on robustness against such names, which command is best?
rubric: NUL-delimited output with `xargs -0` is the only option immune to spaces and newlines in names.
Unquoted substitution and newline-delimited `xargs` split on whitespace; the `ls` loop also splits and is not recursive.

items.prompt: A colleague says: "Putting `set -e` at the top guarantees the script stops at any failing command." Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: It works for external programs, but builtins like `cd` and `echo` return success even on failure, so their errors cannot trigger an exit.
It is sound, though it also aborts on output written to stderr, so it is too strict for scripts that call noisy but harmless tools.
It is sound for simple commands, but it takes effect only when run as `bash -e script`, because the setting inside the file is ignored after the shebang.
It is unreliable: failures in `if` conditions, `&&`/`||` lists and non-final pipeline stages are ignored, so key steps need explicit checks.

rubric: `set -e` is suppressed in conditional contexts and for earlier pipeline stages, so it is not a guarantee.
Distractors invent restrictions (command-line only, builtins exempt, stderr-triggered) that do not match the actual rules.

items.prompt: A cron job runs every minute but sometimes takes over a minute. Criteria: runs must never overlap, and a crash or reboot must never leave a stale lock that blocks future runs. Which approach best meets both?

options.label: `pgrep job.sh || ./job.sh`, because matching process names identifies a running instance without needing any lock file
`flock -n /run/lock/job.lock ./job.sh`, because the kernel releases the lock automatically when the holding process dies
`[ -e /tmp/job.lock ] || { touch /tmp/job.lock; ./job.sh; rm /tmp/job.lock; }`, because a plain lock file is simple and portable
`./job.sh &` followed by `sleep 60`, because pacing each launch at one minute keeps successive runs from ever colliding

rubric: `flock` ties the lock to an open file descriptor, so it vanishes on crash and acquisition is atomic.
The touch-file approach goes stale after a crash and has a race; `pgrep` is racy and name-fragile; sleeping does not prevent overlap.

items.prompt: A script runs `curl -sf "$URL" | sort | wc -l`. Criterion: with the smallest change, the pipeline's exit status must reveal a failure of `curl`, not only of `wc`. Which change best does this?

options.label: Append `2>&1` to the pipeline, because merging stderr into stdout also merges the stage statuses into one
Enable `set -o pipefail`, because the pipeline then returns the last failing stage's status
Add `set -e` alone, because it makes the shell check the status of every stage in a pipeline, not just the last
Test `$?` right after the pipeline, because it holds the status of the first stage that ran in it

rubric: `pipefail` makes the pipeline status reflect any failing stage.
`$?` reports only the last stage, and `set -e` without `pipefail` also sees only the last stage; redirection does not combine statuses.

items.prompt: A shared directory `/srv/proj` is owned by group `devs`. Criteria: new files inherit group `devs`, members can create files, others get no access, and members cannot delete each other's files. Which directory mode is the best fit?

options.label: `chmod 1777`: sticky stops members deleting each other's files, and world write lets everyone create files in the group
`chmod 3770`: setgid keeps the group on new files, and the sticky bit stops members deleting each other's files
`chmod 1770`: sticky stops members deleting each other's files, and the group propagates to new files automatically
`chmod 2770`: setgid keeps the group on new files, and group write already stops members deleting each other's files

rubric: Mode 3770 combines setgid (group inheritance) and sticky (deletion limited to owner), with no access for others.
2770 lets any writer delete others' files; 1770 lacks inheritance; 1777 opens the directory to everyone.

items.prompt: A 40 GB log was removed with `rm` while a daemon (PID 812) is still writing to it. `df` shows no space freed, and the daemon cannot be restarted until the maintenance window. Judged on freeing space now without a restart, which action is best?

options.label: Run `rm -f` on the same path again, because the first removal only unlinked a cached name
Run `sync` to flush dirty buffers to disk, because pending writes keep the deleted file's blocks reserved until flushed
Truncate it via the open descriptor, e.g. `: > /proc/812/fd/4`, because the open handle keeps the inode alive
Run `fsck -f` on the mounted filesystem, because it reclaims orphaned inodes while in use

rubric: A deleted file's blocks persist while a process holds it open; truncating through /proc/PID/fd frees them live.
`sync`, repeated `rm` and `fsck` do not release space held by an open descriptor.

items.prompt: A script starts with `#!/bin/sh` and must run unmodified where `/bin/sh` is dash (strict POSIX). Judged against that criterion, which constructs violate it? Select all that apply.
rubric: Double brackets, arrays and process substitution are bashisms that dash rejects.
`[ ... ]` and `$(...)` are POSIX and work in dash.

items.prompt: Assemble a command listing the 20 largest files over 100 MB in `/data` modified within the last 7 days, size first, largest first, with names containing spaces intact. Which command meets every constraint?
rubric: `-mtime -7` selects recent files, `sort -rn` puts largest first and `head` keeps the top 20.
The distractors use `+7` (older files), ascending sort, or `tail` (smallest files).

items.prompt: Design the temp-file handling for a script. Constraints: the work directory name must be unpredictable, and it must be removed on normal exit, on error exit and on Ctrl-C. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: `tmp=/tmp/job.$$` and a final `rm -rf "$tmp"` as the last line of the script
`tmp=$(mktemp -d)` followed by `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' INT` near the top of the script
`tmp=$(mktemp -d)` followed by `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT` near the top of the script
`tmp=$(mktemp -d)` followed by `trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' KILL` near the top of the script

rubric: `mktemp -d` gives an unpredictable name and an EXIT trap runs on normal exit, errors and handled signals like INT.
The `$$` name is predictable and the final `rm` is skipped on failure; KILL cannot be trapped; INT alone misses normal exit.

items.prompt: In bash, `./build` must show stdout and stderr on the terminal, while also saving stdout to `out.log` and stderr to `err.log`, kept separate. Which redirection assembles this?
rubric: Process substitution gives each stream its own `tee`, and `>&2` keeps stderr on stderr.
Other forms mix streams into both files, redirect tee's own stderr, or send stdout only to the file.

items.prompt: A backup script has `set -eu` and then `mysqldump "$DB" | gzip > "$OUT"`. Constraint: the script must exit non-zero whenever `mysqldump` fails. Which single line is missing?
rubric: Without `pipefail`, only `gzip`'s status counts, so a failed dump yields a success exit.
`set -x` only traces, `umask` affects permissions, and a cleanup trap does not change the exit status.

items.prompt: Assemble a safe batch rename of every `*.jpeg` file in a directory to `.jpg`, where names may contain spaces or begin with a dash. Which loop meets the constraints?
rubric: A glob, quoted expansions, `--` and suffix removal handle spaces and leading dashes.
Parsing `ls` or leaving expansions unquoted splits names; `mv *.jpeg *.jpg` does not rename in bulk.

items.prompt: You must run `uptime` on each of 200 hostnames listed one per line in `hosts.txt`. Constraints: at most 4 SSH sessions at once, and `ssh` must not swallow the host list from stdin. Which command assembles a solution meeting both?

options.label: `while read h; do ssh $h uptime; done < hosts.txt`
`for h in $(cat hosts.txt); do ssh $h uptime & done`

rubric: `xargs -P 4` caps concurrency and `ssh -n` stops ssh reading stdin.
The `while read` loop lets ssh eat the list and is serial; the `&` loop starts all 200 at once; `-n 4` passes the wrong arguments.

items.prompt: Design a cron entry for a script that runs every minute. Constraints: no overlapping runs, errors must be recorded, and it must work in cron's minimal environment. Which elements belong in the design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Launch the job with a trailing `&` so cron never waits
Wrap the command in `flock -n` on a lock file
Append stderr to a log with `2>>/var/log/job.log`
End the script with `sleep 60` to space out runs
Use absolute paths or set `PATH` explicitly

rubric: `flock` prevents overlap, explicit paths cover cron's minimal PATH, and a stderr log records errors.
Sleeping or backgrounding does not prevent overlap and does not address logging or environment.
